newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Waiting in wings, Russian premier brushes up image.
newsitem.headline: Waiting in wings, Russian premier brushes up image.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, waiting quietly in the wings behind ailing President Boris Yeltsin, is discreetly brushing up his image as a man to trust while others around him scramble for power.

Chernomyrdin, 58, is projecting an image of calm and stability in the Kremlin, steadying the ship while Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery and steadfastly avoiding saying anything that suggests he wants to become president.

A television interview which provided a rare glimpse of Chernomyrdin's personal life on Monday night portrayed the former gas industry chief as a likeable, healthy and trustworthy man from humble origins who can be tough when he must be.
Chernomyrdin looked every bit a presidential candidate without saying it -- a man stealthily creeping up on the job rather than trying to yank it from Yeltsin's grasp.

"Chernomyrdin's tactic is to wait and he gains a lot by waiting. He is not a man who likes taking risks and would not pull the rug out from under Yeltsin's feet," independent political analyst Lilia Shevtsova told Reuters.
"He probably could not win an election right now or in three months time, so his best bet is to hope the situation muddles along with him effectively the acting president."
Yeltsin, 65, has already handed Chernomyrdin some of his powers and the prime minister will assume all his duties when he has his heart bypass operation due next month.
It is not clear how long Chernomyrdin will have these formal powers but he and Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais already share a lot of power in Yeltsin's absence.
The next presidential election is due in the year 2000. It would be held sooner if Yeltsin proved unable to govern but the uncharismatic Chernomyrdin is keen to avoid this.

"Right now, Chernomyrdin can act as prime minister and president," said political analyst Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of the USA and Canada Institute thinktank." It would be wrong to think he is not engaged (in the succession struggle)."
Chernomyrdin has quietly, and legitimately, garnered more power as Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery.
He runs a commission which is clamping down on tax-dodging companies, chairs meetings of the Security Council of top leaders and presides over the advisory Defence Council.
He has also signalled his intention to step up his role in ending the conflict in rebel Chechnya by pledging to go to the region for talks for the first time since fighting began.
Chernomyrdin's strengths are his solid record as an economic manager, which has won the respect of the West, and an ability to survive in stormy political waters.

He demonstrated this over the past four months by avoiding getting drawn into open conflicts with Alexander Lebed, whose overt ambitions undermined the authority of both Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin until he was fired as security chief this month.
Chernomyrdin has also clung to power by avoiding scandals, concealing his political ambitions and being loyal to Yeltsin.
"Chernomyrdin showed himself to be just as I expected -- solid and reliable. He did not let me down in a single critical or tough situation," Yeltsin wrote in his 1994 autobiography.
If Chernomyrdin is ever to become president, and many doubt he could beat more charismatic figures such as Lebed at the polls, he must shake off his image as a grey bureaucrat.

Rumours that he accumulated vast wealth as head of the Gazprom natural gas monopoly, which he denies, and his role in the tough economic reforms that have been made since Yeltsin appointed him in December 1992 have also dented his popularity.

Other question marks remain after his Our Home is Russia political party won just slightly over 10 percent in the 1995 parliamentary elections and the threat of economic crisis in the months ahead could adversely affect his political fortunes.
But Monday's interview with commercial NTV television went some way to improving his image and, even if unwittingly, looked like an election campaign broadcast.
Chernomyrdin played the piano accordion, revealed his favourite recipe, held his grandson on his knee and was shown in a photograph riding a jet-ski -- a healthy contrast to Yeltsin.
He expressed a liking for an occasional tipple of vodka and said he regretted not having more time for beautiful women.
